learning: If the oval holds at 20/20 near 1.65 s with equal or lower oscillation, lower yaw inertia is safe and a further small reduction can be tested. If the oval falls or oscillation rises above about 0.2, yaw inertia was damping the baseline controller, and the 0.16 m body should be kept as the reference. If the bends are unchanged, the bend limit is controller-side (gains or base speed).
notes: Complete package for the body_length 0.12 m test. Geometry matches the Builder's proposal exactly, and the controller is the iteration-0 baseline unchanged so the body length is the only variable.
rationale: The Builder's entity0 is a single-variable test: body_length goes from 0.16 to 0.12 m, which cuts yaw inertia by about 25 percent (0.0452 to 0.0340 kg m^2 with 0.6 kg and 0.14 m width). Nothing else changes. Body length does not enter the off-track limit or the sensing, so the only physical effect is turn response. Race evidence: iteration 0 is still the best design (356.6). Its oval finishes 20/20 at 1.65 s with oscillation 0.15, and its s-bend (0.17) and slalom (0.12) fail at max_error about 0.061 m. Sensor lead (y 0.03 and 0.07), footprint (8 mm), spread with a lighter drivetrain, and lighter mass all collapsed or degraded the oval, so the controller appears tuned to the baseline. The controller therefore stays exactly at the iteration-0 baseline (kp 2.5, ki 0.05, kd 0.3, base_speed 1.8, weights [2,1,0,-1,-2], last_direction), so the geometry is the only variable. I expect the oval to stay near 20/20 at about 1.65 s, with steering oscillation at or below 0.15 because the shorter body reduces yaw response. Bend progress may rise slightly. This is untested, and if the oval falls, the baseline body length remains the reference.
